checkpoint.tractability_note: 1847428 parameters, not a 1.2B language model, which is why a fine-tune is tractable here at all and why this is NOT comparable to this project's blocked large-LM fine-tunes.

comparator.comparison: the fine-tuned encoder's median Spearman against the FROZEN encoder's 0.5076 on byte-identical splits

early_stop.why: the best epoch is followed by 8 non-improving epochs against a required patience of 2, so the curve HAS turned and the epoch budget is bounded by observation

convergence.scope: a SUBSAMPLE curve. It bounds the SHAPE of convergence, NOT the full-cohort epoch count, because measuring the latter is the expensive run this probe exists to size.

convergence_sizing.why: the EPOCH COUNT is the target and the subsample is derived to fit it, because the curve's shape lives on the epoch axis; a bigger subsample at the same epoch count would only raise the curve's level

deviation_rule: a deviation is allowed; an UNRECORDED deviation raises. Every key that differs from the checkpoint's own config carries its reason here.

deviations_from_pretraining_recipe.why: the pretraining batch of 1024 was used on a CUDA device for a masked language-model objective. This host is CPU-only with 4 threads, and the throughput was MEASURED across batch sizes rather than assumed: 128 is the fastest of {'32': 24.7, '64': 23.7, '128': 27.0}, so it is the batch the arm uses AND the rate the projection is computed from. Bigger is not faster here.
the pretraining budget of 2000 epochs is for the masked LM objective on the full corpus; this is a bounded convergence OBSERVATION sized from the measured throughput

the pretraining patience of 25 is calibrated to a 2000-epoch budget; a subsample curve of 15 epochs cannot express it, so the probe uses a proportionate value and the artifact reports whether the curve turned under it

route.ceiling_is_operational_not_statistical: six hours is chosen because an overnight run is recoverable while a multi-day local run on 4 CPU threads tends to be abandoned part-way, which yields a PARTIAL artifact nobody can read. A reader may disagree with the number explicitly; it is a constant, not a judgement made per run.
route.why: the projected local cost 23.82 h EXCEEDS the named ceiling of 6.00 h by 4.0x, so the arm routes to a Kaggle T4 rather than being started locally and abandoned part-way.

target_transform.source: dna_decode.glm.atlas_embed.ridge_spearman, which fits on log1p(expression) and scores Spearman against RAW expression, and whose docstring states that any deviation makes the number incomparable with the committed incumbent tables
target_transform.why_it_matters: training on RAW expression instead would confound the OBJECTIVE TRANSFORM with the REPRESENTATION, adding a third reading to the budget-versus-representation pair: a loss could mean the fine-tune optimised the wrong target scale. Fixed before this measurement, not after.

the_two_readings_that_must_not_be_confla: Beating 0.5076 shows the frozen REPRESENTATION was the limit. Failing to beat it shows the SUBSTRATE or the TRAINING BUDGET was -- and a budget-limited null is NOT a representation-limited one. The `convergence.early_stop.turned` field is what distinguishes them: if the curve never turned, a null is uninterpretable.

throughput.note: the first step of each batch size is discarded; a cold step includes lazy allocator and kernel-selection cost and would understate the sustained rate
throughput.rate_and_batch_come_from_the_SAME_row: The projected cost uses the rate measured AT the batch size the arm will use. Taking the fastest rate across batch sizes while training at a different one understates the cost -- on this host by about 1.7x, since batch 32 measures ~40 seq/s and batch 64 ~24 seq/s. So the chosen batch size IS the fastest measured one, which makes the two consistent by construction rather than by coincidence.

verdict_detail: throughput, convergence and route are all measured: best epoch 6 of 15, followed by 8 non-improving epochs, routed to kaggle_t4.
